lead: FM generation is the process of making a carrier's instantaneous frequency follow the message. There are two routes. A direct generator pulls the frequency of an oscillator with a voltage, using a varactor diode, a reactance modulator or a voltage-controlled oscillator. An indirect generator starts with narrowband FM, multiplies carrier and deviation together, then mixes the carrier to the final channel while leaving deviation alone. Direct circuits are simple but drift; indirect circuits are stable because a crystal sets the initial carrier. FM broadcast transmitters, two-way radios and software-defined radios all use one of these ideas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for β and Carson's rule, and Unit 2 for the mixer and superheterodyne idea.

sections.h3: Direct FM: voltage controls the oscillator

blocks.text: In direct FM the message voltage is applied inside the oscillator. The tuned circuit that sets the frequency contains a component whose value changes with voltage. The oscillator frequency then changes at the same rate as the message. This is a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO).

The common component is a varactor diode. It is a p-n junction operated in reverse bias, so it acts as a capacitor. Its capacitance falls as reverse voltage rises. Connect it across the LC tank; the message changes C, so the resonant frequency changes. The relation is:

blocks.where: f₀ is the centre frequency in hertz; L is the tank inductance in henry; C(V) is the total tank capacitance in farad, including the varactor; V is the message voltage in volt.

blocks.text: A reactance modulator uses a transistor or FET with a feedback network so that its input looks like a reactance across the tank. The message changes the device transconductance, which changes the effective reactance and hence frequency. It can give larger deviation than a simple varactor.

Two practical limits matter. First, C(V) is nonlinear, so equal message steps do not give equal frequency steps. Keep deviation small or linearise with a correction network. Second, the centre frequency drifts with temperature, bias and supply. An automatic frequency control (AFC) loop compares the oscillator with a stable crystal reference and corrects the bias. Without AFC, a direct FM transmitter can wander off channel.

The Armstrong method avoids a drifting power oscillator. A crystal oscillator feeds a narrowband FM (NBFM) modulator. NBFM has small β, so it is easy to make linearly by a phase modulator. The initial deviation is tiny.
A frequency multiplier by N multiplies every frequency in the wave: carrier and deviation. So:
f_c′ = N f_c,  Δf′ = N Δf,  β′ = N β
blocks.where: f_c is the input carrier in hertz; Δf is the input peak deviation in hertz; β is the modulation index; N is the integer multiplier; primed values are after multiplication.

blocks.text: A mixer then adds or subtracts a local oscillator frequency. It shifts the carrier only: f_c″ = |f_c′ ± f_LO|, while Δf″ = Δf′. The deviation does not grow because the mixer is a frequency translation, not a frequency multiplication. A band-pass filter selects the sum or difference, and an RF amplifier feeds the antenna.
The order matters: multiply first to get the deviation you need, then mix to the assigned channel. If you mix first, later multiplication would multiply the already-correct deviation and overdeviate.

sections.h3: Design arithmetic and FM/PM conversion rules

blocks.text: The design uses the tone relation Δf = β f_m. Here Δf is peak deviation in hertz, β is modulation index, and f_m is message frequency in hertz. The multiplier needed is N = Δf_target / Δf_NBFM. The carrier after multiplication is N f_c, and after mixing is N f_c ± f_LO. β after multiplication is N β_NBFM.

For example, a 15 kHz message with β = 0.1 at 100 kHz has NBFM deviation 1.5 kHz. A multiplier of 50 gives 5 MHz and 75 kHz deviation. A 95 MHz local oscillator then gives 100 MHz by the sum, while deviation stays 75 kHz. The worked example below shows every step.

The same hardware can convert FM and PM. To generate FM with a phase modulator, integrate the message first: feed m(t) through an integrator, because phase is the integral of frequency. To generate PM with a frequency modulator, differentiate the message first, because frequency is the derivative of phase. These two rules explain why the same modulator block can be labelled FM or PM.

In a software-defined radio the VCO is replaced by a numerically controlled oscillator. The message updates a frequency control word, so the phase accumulator runs faster or slower. The arithmetic is the same as direct FM; the limits are digital word length and DAC clocks. Simple varactor circuits remain common in low-cost transmitters.

spec.title: Armstrong indirect FM
spec.aria: A 100 kHz NBFM wave with 1.5 kHz deviation is multiplied by 50 to give 5 MHz and 75 kHz deviation, then mixed up to 100 MHz without changing the deviation.

examples.question: Design an Armstrong transmitter for 100 MHz with Δf = 75 kHz using a 15 kHz message. The NBFM stage has a 100 kHz carrier and β = 0.1.
steps: For a tone, β = Δf / f_m, so Δf_NBFM = β f_m = 0.1 × 15 kHz = 1.5 kHz.
The required deviation ratio is N = Δf_target / Δf_NBFM = 75 kHz / 1.5 kHz = 50.
Use a ×50 multiplier. Carrier becomes 100 kHz × 50 = 5 MHz. Deviation becomes 1.5 kHz × 50 = 75 kHz.
The modulation index after multiplication is β′ = N β = 50 × 0.1 = 5. This matches Δf_target / f_m = 75 kHz / 15 kHz = 5.
Mix with a 95 MHz local oscillator and select the sum: 5 MHz + 95 MHz = 100 MHz. The difference 90 MHz is rejected by the filter.
The mixer does not multiply frequency, so deviation remains 75 kHz. Feed the 100 MHz, 75 kHz wave to the RF amplifier.
examples.answer: The Armstrong transmitter uses a ×50 multiplier after a 100 kHz NBFM stage with 1.5 kHz deviation, then a 95 MHz mixer; the output is 100 MHz with 75 kHz deviation.
examples.check:
fm = 15e3
beta_nbfm = 0.1
fc_nbfm = 100e3
target_dev = 75e3
dev_nbfm = beta_nbfm * fm
N = target_dev / dev_nbfm
fc_mult = fc_nbfm * N
dev_mult = dev_nbfm * N
beta_mult = N * beta_nbfm
lo = 95e6
fc_out = fc_mult + lo
dev_out = dev_mult
print(fc_out)
print(dev_out)

code.code:
fm = 15e3
beta = 0.1
fc = 100e3
dev = beta * fm
N = 75e3 / dev
fc2 = fc * N
dev2 = dev * N
lo = 95e6
print(fc2 + lo)
print(dev2)

traps: A multiplier scales carrier and deviation together. A mixer shifts carrier only. Mixing cannot increase deviation; only a multiplier or a higher-β modulator can.
β = Δf / f_m, not Δf × f_m. Doubling message frequency at fixed deviation halves β.
Varactor capacitance versus voltage is nonlinear; a large direct-FM deviation produces distortion unless linearised.
Centre-frequency drift and deviation are different faults. AFC corrects slow drift of the centre, not the audio deviation.
In Armstrong design, multiply before mixing. If the final mixer is placed before the multiplier, the multiplier will multiply the already-final deviation and overdeviate.

quiz.q: What is a varactor diode used for in direct FM?
quiz.a: It is a reverse-biased p-n junction used as a voltage-controlled capacitor across the LC tank; the message changes its capacitance and hence the oscillator frequency.

quiz.q: Why is an AFC loop needed in a direct FM transmitter?
quiz.a: Temperature, bias and supply changes drift the centre frequency. AFC compares the oscillator with a crystal reference and corrects the bias to hold the centre.

quiz.q: An NBFM stage has carrier 200 kHz, deviation 2 kHz and β = 0.2. A ×100 multiplier follows. Find the new carrier, deviation and β.
quiz.a: Carrier = 200 kHz × 100 = 20 MHz. Deviation = 2 kHz × 100 = 200 kHz. β = 0.2 × 100 = 20.

quiz.q: A 5 MHz FM wave with 75 kHz deviation and 15 kHz message is mixed to 100 MHz. What happens to deviation and β?
quiz.a: The mixer shifts only the carrier. Deviation stays 75 kHz. Because f_m is unchanged, β = 75 kHz / 15 kHz = 5 also stays unchanged.

quiz.q: State the main difference between direct and indirect FM generation.
quiz.a: Direct FM changes the oscillator frequency directly with the message. Indirect FM makes NBFM, multiplies carrier and deviation by N, then mixes the carrier to the final frequency.

quiz.q: To get 60 kHz deviation from an NBFM stage with 1.5 kHz deviation, what multiplier is needed? If its carrier is 150 kHz, what is the multiplied carrier?
quiz.a: N = 60 kHz / 1.5 kHz = 40. Multiplied carrier = 150 kHz × 40 = 6 MHz.

quiz.q: Why must the message be integrated before a phase modulator when FM is wanted?
quiz.a: A phase modulator makes carrier phase proportional to its input. Frequency is the derivative of phase. Integrating the message makes phase proportional to ∫m(t)dt, so instantaneous frequency becomes proportional to m(t), which is FM.

quiz.q: Give the two FM/PM conversion rules.
quiz.a: FM from PM: integrate the message before the phase modulator. PM from FM: differentiate the message before the frequency modulator.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real FM chips often use a fractional-N phase-locked loop as the VCO, giving both stable channel selection and direct modulation. Software-defined radios generate FM entirely in digital phase accumulators and use the same multiplier-and-mixer arithmetic for upconversion. Chirp radar and spread-spectrum systems also sweep frequency, so the linearity limits of direct FM matter there.
